title: Grace perfects nature (ST I.1.8)
hook: grace doesn't destroy nature but brings it to completion

segments.voice: Yesterday, how the Summa works: objections, on the contrary, I answer that, and replies. Your line was state the other side first. Whose point did you say back to them before you answered? Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

A piano tuner arrives at an old upright that hasn't been touched in years. She doesn't saw it in half. She doesn't swap it for a synthesizer. She opens the lid, finds the strings and hammers that are already there, and works on them one by one, until the instrument sounds the way it was built to sound. Same wood. Same keys. Only now, finished. Thomas Aquinas has a short line that works like that tuner. It's tucked into a reply, early in the Summa, and it shapes how he holds faith and reason, God and the ordinary human person. Today's word is that line.
screen: `AN OLD PIANO.` → `NOT SAWN IN HALF.` → `BROUGHT TO PITCH.`

segments.voice: It comes in the Summa's very first question, at the eighth article: does sacred teaching argue? Thomas says yes. Not to prove the faith, which rests on what God has revealed, but to start from it and make other things clear. Then he meets an objection. If faith rests on God's word, doesn't bringing in human reason cheapen it? His reply, put plainly: grace does not destroy nature, it perfects it. So natural reason should serve faith, the way the will's natural leaning serves love. Unpack the two words. Nature is what a thing is, what it's made with. For a person, that's a mind that asks why, a body, a temperament, hands that can learn a craft. Grace is God's free gift. Now there are two pictures Thomas sets aside. In one, grace is a bulldozer: to be holy, stop being human. Flatten the mind, scorn the body. In the other, grace is a sticker: something pasted on top that leaves you just as you were. Thomas's picture is the tuner. Grace works on what's already there and brings it to completion. And he shows it in the same reply. He notes that Paul, preaching in Athens, quotes one of the Greeks' own poets. In the Douay-Rheims, Acts gives Paul's words: "as some also of your own poets said: For we are also his offspring." A pagan poet's line, put to work for the gospel. Reason didn't have to be thrown out. It was given a job. On an ordinary day, this is why Catholic teaching can say that your curiosity, your humor, your patience with a tangled knot are not rivals to holiness. Catholics say grace takes them further than they could go alone.
screen: `DOES SACRED TEACHING ARGUE?` · `GRACE DOES NOT DESTROY NATURE.` · `NOT A BULLDOZER, NOT A STICKER.` · `PAUL QUOTES A GREEK POET.` · then, large: `FOR WE ARE ALSO HIS OFFSPRING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks for your natural gifts. Settle, and breathe. Name one thing you were simply made with. A quick mind. Steady hands. A good ear. A knack for putting people at ease. Don't be modest, and don't boast either. Just name it the way you'd name the color of your eyes. Then a second gift, and a third, if they come. Notice that you didn't earn them. If you pray, you can thank God for each one, by name. If you don't, simply hold them for a moment as things given. The bell holds the time.
Grace perfects nature. Thomas Aquinas's line from the Summa's first question: God's gift doesn't wipe out what we are, it brings it to completion. Today's word.
Your line: grace completes. Today, use one of the gifts you named on purpose, for someone else, and notice what it's for. Day one thousand one hundred fifty-four.

howItsDone: Catholic teachers often use Thomas's line that grace perfects nature to explain why the Church values reason, science, art and ordinary human gifts alongside faith.

original.script: gratia non tollat naturam, sed perficiat
original.say: GRAH-tsee-ah non TOL-laht nah-TOO-rahm, sed per-FEE-chee-aht
original.note: Latin, from Summa I.1.8: grace does not take away nature, but perfects it.

trapdoor: what you thought: grace turns you into someone else.
what it means: God's gift works on what you are made with and brings it to completion.
what a scholar hears: a reply to an objection in Summa I.1.8: reason serves faith as the will's natural leaning serves love, with Paul quoting a poet as the example.

notes: ST I.1.8 paraphrased: sacred doctrine argues from the articles of faith, not to prove them; reply 2: since grace does not destroy nature but perfects it, natural reason should minister to faith as the natural bent of the will ministers to charity; Paul quoting a poet (Thomas names Aratus) at Acts 17:28. Confirm.

Original: Thomas's Latin is 'cum enim gratia non tollat naturam, sed perficiat'; the commonly cited form 'gratia non tollit naturam, sed perficit eam' is a later summary. Confirm the form given and the pronunciation.
The bulldozer and sticker pictures are the script's own illustrations, not Thomas's.
'Catholics say grace takes them further' — confirm this fairly summarizes Catholic teaching on grace and natural gifts.
